title: Pay, rosters and future jobs at heart of WA's latest coal strike
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Pay, rosters and future jobs at heart of WA's latest coal strike

More than 100 mine workers have gathered in Collie, accusing Chinese-owned Premier Coal and the WA government of failing to heed their concerns over pay and their future employment prospects.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC South West WA

Topic:Coal

About 100 coal mine workers have walked off the job in Collie after rejecting an offer from Premier Coal. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

Workers at one of WA's two remaining coal mines have walked off the job, citing concerns over pay and their future employment prospects.

More than 100 staff from Premier Coal took part in the two-hour stoppage ahead of the 2030 shutdown of state-owned coal fired power generation in WA.

Premier Coal says it remains committed to reaching a fair and sustainable deal with its remaining workforce.

More than 100 mine workers have been joined by Collie residents in a push for higher wages ahead  of the WA government's planned shutdown of coal-fired power generation in the state.

The workers from Chinese-owned Premier Coal, the main supplier to the state-owned Muja and Collie power plants, began a two-hour work stoppage at 4pm on Tuesday.

The state government has promised to shutter both power stations, located 200km south of Perth at the heart of the state's largest electricity grid, by 2030, despite doubts over replacement generation.

The Mining and Energy Union said workers were opposed to proposed roster changes, some of which, it said, could result in staff losing about $30,000 a year in penalty rates.

The union says the offer from Premier Coal could leave workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

MEU district secretary Greg Busson estimated average annual salary sat at about $150,000 a year, with more than 90 per cent of the mine's workforce unionised.

While Premier had offered a twelve per cent increase spread over four years, Mr Busson said the union wanted any increase front-loaded.

Premier Coal operates one of WA's two remaining coal mines, both of which are located in Collie. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)

"Depending on which roster the company choose to move to, it could mean up to $30,000 a year reduction in people's wages," Mr Busson said.

Workers now work 12-hour shifts on a four-days on, four-days off, four-nights on, four-nights off rotation.

Mr Busson said two of the proposed rosters would effectively end night shifts and associated penalties.

"The worst [roster] is 8.5 hours all-day shift, Monday to Friday, because they lose all their penalties for weekends and night shift," he said.

A Premier Coal spokesperson said the company was committed to reaching a fair agreement.

"Premier Coal has participated in good faith negotiations throughout the enterprise bargaining process," the spokesperson said.

"Our focus remains on the safety of our workforce and the continuation of safe and efficient operations."

A Premier Coal spokesperson says the company intends to continue negotiating in good faith. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

Mr Busson said $150,000 a year might seem a generous salary, but the work was often dangerous and the pay was less than that taken home by coal workers in other states.

He said workers were also anxious about finding other opportunities in the town as mining operations wound down.

Collie has been the heart of coal mining and power generation in WA for more than a century. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

Mr Busson said that was despite the state government spending more than $700 million on a transition fund to help the town survive the end of coal.

"As hard as the government is trying, we haven't got any new industries in Collie yet," he said.

A state government spokesperson said a number of industries in the Collie Basin were being supported and pointed to the creation of 500 jobs during the construction of Synergy's big battery.

Workers have stepped up calls for clarity around WA's transition away from coal-fired power. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)
